cor-lm-cov-estimate.title: Estimated covariance and standard errors
cor-lm-cov-estimate.html: Under the conditions of @thm-lm-sigma2, s2(X⊤X)−1 is an unbiased estimator of 𝛃Cov(β^), and s2a⊤(X⊤X)−1a is an unbiased estimator of 𝛃Var(a⊤β^). The standard error of β^j is se(β^j)=s[(X⊤X)−1]jj.

cor-lm-linear-functions.title: Linear functions of the coefficients
cor-lm-linear-functions.html: Under the assumptions of @thm-lm-moments(b), let a∈Rp and let L be a constant q×p matrix. Then 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(a⊤β^)=a⊤β,Var(a⊤β^)=σ2a⊤(X⊤X)−1a, and 𝛃Cov(Lβ^)=σ2L(X⊤X)−1L⊤. In particular, the estimated mean response at a design point x0, 𝛃μ^0=x0⊤β^, is unbiased for 𝛃μ0=x0⊤β with Var(μ^0)=σ2x0⊤(X⊤X)−1x0, and Var(β^j)=σ2[(X⊤X)−1]jj.

cor-lm-random-regressors.title: Random regressors
cor-lm-random-regressors.html: Let (X,Y) be random, with rank(X)=p with probability one, and suppose 𝛃E(Y∣X)=Xβ and Cov(Y∣X)=σ2In. If E[(X⊤X)−1] is finite, then 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(β^)=β,Cov(β^)=σ2E[(X⊤X)−1].

cor-lm-s2-consistent.title: Consistency of s²
cor-lm-s2-consistent.html: Under the conditions of @prp-lm-var-s2, Var(s2)≤2σ4+|μ4−3σ4|n−p. So if n−p→∞ along a sequence of models, s2→σ2 in mean square and in probability.

cor-lm-simple-moments.title: Moments for a straight line
cor-lm-simple-moments.html:
In the model @eq-lm-simple-model with Sxx>0, Var(β^1)=σ2Sxx,Var(β^0)=σ2(1n+x¯2Sxx),Cov(β^0,β^1)=−σ2x¯Sxx, and the estimated mean response at x0 has Var(β^0+β^1x0)=σ2(1n+(x0−x¯)2Sxx).{#eq-lm-var-mean-response}

Both estimates are unbiased, and Y¯ is uncorrelated with β^1.

def-lm-coefficient-interpretation.title: Interpretation of a coefficient
def-lm-coefficient-interpretation.html:
In a linear model E(Y∣x)=β0+β1x1+⋯+βkxk, suppose the regressor xj enters the model only through its own column, so that no other column is a function of xj. For any two regressor profiles x and x′ that agree in every regressor except the jth, and have xj′=xj+1, E(Y∣x′)−E(Y∣x)=βj.{#eq-lm-partial-effect}

The coefficient βj is the partial effect of xj in this model: the difference in mean response per unit difference in xj, between profiles that agree on all the other regressors in the model. Its estimate β^j is the least squares estimate of this difference.

def-lm-least-squares.title: Least squares estimate
def-lm-least-squares.html: For an n×p matrix X and y∈Rn, the least squares criterion is S(b)=‖y−Xb‖2=∑i=1n(yi−x(i)⊤b)2,b∈Rp. A least squares estimate of 𝛃β is any 𝛃β^ that minimizes S. The corresponding fitted values are 𝛃Y^=Xβ^, the residuals are 𝛆𝛃ε^=y−Xβ^, and the residual sum of squares is 𝛃𝛆SSE=S(β^)=‖ε^‖2.

def-lm-linear-model.title: The linear model
def-lm-linear-model.html:
The linear model for a random vector Y∈Rn is 𝛃𝛆𝛆𝛆Y=Xβ+ε,E(ε)=0,Cov(ε)=σ2In,{#eq-lm-model}

where the model matrix X is a known n×p matrix of constants, and the coefficient vector 𝛃β∈Rp and the error variance σ2>0 are unknown parameters. The conditions on 𝛆ε are the second-moment assumptions. If in addition 𝛆ε∼Nn(0,σ2In), equivalently 𝛃Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2In), the model is the normal linear model. The model has full rank if rank(X)=p.

def-lm-regression-function.title: Regression function
def-lm-regression-function.html: The regression function of Y on X is the conditional mean m(x)=E(Y∣X=x). The error is ε=Y−m(X), so that Y=m(X)+ε.

eq-lm-beta-hat.html: 𝛃β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y;

eq-lm-cov-beta.html: 𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2(X⊤X)−1.

eq-lm-hat-matrix.html: 𝛃Y^=Xβ^=Hy,H=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤,

eq-lm-interaction.html: E(Y)=β0+β1x1+β2x2+β3x1x2=(β0+β2x2)+(β1+β3x2)x1,

eq-lm-ls-decomposition.html: 𝛃𝛃𝛃‖y−Xb‖2=‖y−Xβ^‖2+(b−β^)⊤X⊤X(b−β^),

eq-lm-model.html: 𝛃𝛆𝛆𝛆Y=Xβ+ε,E(ε)=0,Cov(ε)=σ2In,

eq-lm-model-moments.html: 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ,Cov(Y)=σ2In.

eq-lm-normal-equations.html: X⊤Xb=X⊤y

eq-lm-partial-effect.html: E(Y∣x′)−E(Y∣x)=βj.

eq-lm-s2.html: 𝛃s2=SSEn−p=‖Y−Xβ^‖2n−p

eq-lm-sandwich.html: 𝛃Cov(β^)=(X⊤X)−1X⊤ΣX(X⊤X)−1.

eq-lm-simple-decomposition.html: S(b0,b1)=S(β^0,β^1)+n[(b0−β^0)+(b1−β^1)x¯]2+Sxx(b1−β^1)2.

eq-lm-simple-estimates.html: β^1=SxySxx,β^0=y¯−β^1x¯.

eq-lm-simple-inverse.html: (X⊤X)−1=1nSxx(∑ixi2−nx¯−nx¯n)=(1n+x¯2Sxx−x¯Sxx−x¯Sxx1Sxx),

eq-lm-simple-model.html: Yi=β0+β1xi+εi,i=1,…,n,

eq-lm-simple-normal.html: ∑i=1n(yi−b0−b1xi)=0,∑i=1nxi(yi−b0−b1xi)=0.

eq-lm-sums.html: x¯=1n∑ixi,y¯=1n∑iyi,Sxx=∑i(xi−x¯)2,Sxy=∑i(xi−x¯)(yi−y¯),Syy=∑i(yi−y¯)2.

eq-lm-toward-mean.html: β^1=rsysx,equivalentlyy^−y¯sy=rx−x¯sx.

eq-lm-var-mean-response.html: Var(β^0+β^1x0)=σ2(1n+(x0−x¯)2Sxx).

exm-lm-co2.title: A curved trend and a seasonal cycle
exm-lm-co2.title_html: A curved trend and a seasonal cycle
exm-lm-co2.html: The monthly mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, from March 1958 to December 2001, gives n=521 observations in parts per million. Let t be the time in years, at the middle of each month, and tc=t−1980. The model E(Y)=β0+β1tc+β2tc2+γ1cos⁡2πt+γ2sin⁡2πt+γ3cos⁡4πt+γ4sin⁡4πt has p=7 columns, and the model matrix has full rank. Its least squares fit (Section 5.4) has β^0=337.6163,β^1=1.3344,β^2=0.0118, γ^1=−1.0413,γ^2=2.5641,γ^3=0.6284,γ^4=−0.3859. The quadratic term says the rate of increase is itself increasing. The slope of the trend, β1+2β2tc, is estimated as 0.86 ppm per year in 1960 and 1.81 ppm per year in 2000. The annual harmonic has amplitude 2.77 ppm and the half-year harmonic 0.74 ppm. Together they make a seasonal swing of 6.0 ppm from the late-spring peak to the autumn trough, as the vegetation of the northern hemisphere takes up carbon over the summer. The residual standard deviation (estimated as in Section 5.6) is 0.760 ppm, against 2.743 ppm for a straight line in time alone. Figure 5.3.1 shows the data, the trend and the seasonal cycle.

exm-lm-counts.title: Physician visits are counts
exm-lm-counts.html:
The number of physician visits in the RAND data is a count. It is zero for 31.2 percent of person-years, and its variance is 7.09 times its mean. Group the person-years into ten groups by the chronic-disease score, and compute the mean and variance of visits in each (Figure 5.8.1). The variance rises with the mean, and in every group it is between 4.8 and 8.8 times the mean. (L2) fails badly.

Two models for the mean are fitted to the disease score x. The linear model gives 1.268+0.1416x visits. The Poisson regression with log link (@def-cnt-poisson) gives exp⁡(0.549+0.0408x): each unit of the index multiplies the mean by e0.0408, 4.17 percent more visits. Over the bulk of the data the two curves are close, and both follow the group means. They differ in shape at high values of the index, where the log-linear mean grows ever faster and the linear one at a constant rate, and where the data are too sparse to decide between them. They differ more in what they assume about variability. The linear model assumes a constant variance; the Poisson model assumes variance equal to the mean. The data contradict both. Chapter 38 shows how to keep the log-linear mean and let the variance be a multiple of it.

The Poisson fit is not computed by ordinary least squares, but its estimating equations have the same form as the normal equations: 𝛍X⊤(y−μ^)=0, where 𝛍μ^ is the vector of fitted means. The residuals are again orthogonal to every column of X. The listing checks this.

exm-lm-designs.title: Where to put the design points
exm-lm-designs.title_html: Where to put the design points
exm-lm-designs.html: Suppose n=20 observations can be taken anywhere in [0,10] to estimate a slope. Three designs are compared in Figure 5.5.1. Equally spaced points give Sxx=184.21 and a slope standard deviation of 0.0737σ. Putting half the points at each end gives the largest possible Sxx=500.00 (@exr-lm-optimal-design) and 0.0447σ. Bunching the points in the middle, over [4,6], gives Sxx=7.37 and 0.3684σ, more than eight times worse than the two-ends design. The simulated sampling distributions in panel (b), each from 20,000 samples, match these standard deviations. The two-ends design has a price the variance formula does not show: with only two distinct values of x, the data cannot reveal curvature. The equally spaced design gives up some precision for the ability to check the model.

exm-lm-divisor.title: How bad is dividing by n?
exm-lm-divisor.title_html: How bad is dividing by n?
exm-lm-divisor.html: Take n=30 cases and model matrices with an intercept and p−1 further columns of standard normal numbers, for p=1,…,25. For each p, 20,000 error vectors are simulated with σ2=1. Figure 5.6.1 plots the average of SSE/n and of SSE/(n−p). The first follows the line (n−p)/n: at p=5 it averages 0.834, at p=15 it averages 0.500, half the true value, and at p=25 only 0.167. The unbiased estimator averages 1.000, 1.001 and 0.999 at the same values of p.

exm-lm-elnino.title: Forecasting December sea temperature
exm-lm-elnino.html:
The Niño 1+2 index is the mean sea surface temperature in a region of the Pacific off Peru and Ecuador. It is high during El Niño events. We use the monthly values for the 61 years 1950–2010 and ask how well the August value predicts the December value four months later. Here x is the August temperature and y the December temperature, both in degrees Celsius. The summary statistics are x¯=20.843,y¯=22.693,Sxx=77.801,Sxy=56.008,Syy=70.380, so by @thm-lm-simple-ls β^1=56.00877.801=0.7199,β^0=22.693−0.7199×20.843=7.6887. Each extra degree in August goes with 0.7199 of a degree more in the following December, on average. For an August temperature of 22°C the fitted December mean is 23.53°C. The intercept, the fitted December temperature after an August at 0°C, is meaningless: no August in the data is below 19°C.

The residual sum of squares is SSE=30.061, and R2=0.5729, the square of the correlation r=0.7569. The slope is less than 1 partly because r<1 and partly because December temperatures vary a little less than August ones: sy=1.083 against sx=1.139.

exm-lm-fixed-random.title: One slope, two sampling schemes
exm-lm-fixed-random.html: Take Y=1+0.5x+ε with standard normal errors and n=15 cases. In the fixed design, the regressor values are drawn once from the uniform distribution on [0,10] and then kept. They have Sxx=∑i(xi−x¯)2=103.73. In the random design, a new set of 15 regressor values is drawn for every sample. Over 50,000 simulated samples, the least squares slope (formula in Section 5.2) averages 0.5007 under the fixed design and 0.5006 under the random one. Both are unbiased. Their variances differ in meaning. Under the fixed design the simulated variance is 0.00960, matching σ2/Sxx=0.00964 for this particular design. Under the random design it is 0.00933, matching the average E(σ2/Sxx)=0.00923 over designs, estimated from the same simulation. Replacing Sxx by its expectation 116.67 would give 0.00857, which is too small. By Jensen’s inequality E(1/Sxx)≥1/E(Sxx), so random bunching of the regressors costs precision on average.

exm-lm-health-adjusted.title: Self-rated health, with and without adjustment
exm-lm-health-adjusted.title_html: Self-rated health, with and without adjustment
exm-lm-health-adjusted.html:
In @exm-lm-health-coding, people reporting poor health made 3.160 more physician visits a year, on average, than those reporting excellent health. Add two regressors: a chronic-disease score (the variable disea) and an indicator of a physical limitation. The coefficient of poor health falls to 1.554, and that of fair health from 1.058 to 0.202. The good-health coefficient changes sign, to −0.081. The adjusted comparison is between people with the same disease score and limitation status. Much of the difference in visits between health categories goes with differences in measured disease, and the self-rating adds less once disease is taken into account. Neither set of numbers is “the” effect of self-rated health. They answer different questions.

The data record the same people in several years, so the cases are not independent and the second-moment assumptions do not hold exactly; Chapter 33 treats such clustered data.

exm-lm-health-coding.title: Self-rated health
exm-lm-health-coding.html: The RAND Health Insurance Experiment recorded, for 20,190 person-years, the number of outpatient visits to a physician and the person’s own rating of their health: excellent, good, fair or poor. With excellent as the reference, the model E(Yi)=β0+β1gi+β2fi+β3qi uses three indicator columns g,f,q for good, fair and poor health. For a person in excellent health the mean is β0; in good health, β0+β1; in fair health, β0+β2; in poor health, β0+β3. So β1,β2,β3 are the differences in mean visits between each category and the reference. @prp-lm-indicator-means shows that the least squares estimates are the corresponding differences of sample means. In these data they are 0.268, 1.058 and 3.160 visits a year, on top of β^0=2.634 for excellent health.

exm-lm-kurtosis.title: Skewed errors inflate the variance of s²
exm-lm-kurtosis.title_html: Skewed errors inflate the variance of s²
exm-lm-kurtosis.html: With n=30 and the first p=6 columns of the model matrix of @exm-lm-divisor, the leverages give ∑i(1−hii)2=19.431. For normal errors with σ2=1, Var(SSE)=2(n−p)=48.00. For centred exponential errors, which have σ2=1 and μ4=9, @prp-lm-var-s2 gives 48+6×19.431=164.59, and a simulation with 200,000 data sets gives 165.19. The standard deviation of s2 is 0.289 under normal errors and 0.535 under exponential errors, nearly twice as large, although s2 is unbiased in both cases.

exm-lm-money.title: Money demand in Denmark
exm-lm-money.html: Economic theory relates the amount of money people choose to hold to their income, which drives the volume of transactions, and to interest rates, which measure the return given up by holding money rather than bonds. A classic data set records, for n=55 quarters from 1974 to 1987 in Denmark, the logarithm of real money holdings (y), the logarithm of real income, the interest rate on bonds and the interest rate on deposits (rates as fractions per year). The model has p=4 columns: an intercept and the three regressors. Solving the normal equations gives 𝛃β^=(4.3945, 1.2958, −2.6163, 0.6186)⊤, with residual sum of squares SSE=0.09253 and R2=0.9262. The listing checks that 𝛆X⊤ε^ is zero up to rounding error, that the two formulas for SSE in @prp-lm-fit-algebra(c) agree, and that the slopes computed from centred data (@prp-lm-centred) are the same. Section 5.6 attaches standard errors to these numbers, and Section 5.7 interprets them.

exm-lm-money-interpret.title: Reading the money demand coefficients
exm-lm-money-interpret.html:
In @exm-lm-money the response is log real money and the first regressor is log real income, so β^1=1.2958 is an income elasticity. Comparing quarters with the same interest rates, 1 percent more real income goes with about 1.3 percent more real money. The interest rates are measured as fractions, so the bond rate coefficient −2.6163 is per unit of the fraction, that is, per 100 percentage points, an absurdly large change. Rescaling the rate to percentage points (@prp-lm-reparameterization with c=100) divides the coefficient by 100: a bond rate one percentage point higher, with income and the deposit rate the same, goes with money holdings lower by the factor e−0.026163, a difference of −2.58 percent. The deposit rate has a positive coefficient, which is plausible if deposits are part of the money measured, since a higher deposit rate makes holding them more attractive. But the coefficient is smaller than its standard error.

The standardized coefficients of income, bond rate and deposit rate are 0.619, −0.529 and 0.057. The sample standard deviation of log income is 0.0728, about 7 percent, and that of the bond rate is 0.0308, about 3 percentage points; within those ranges of variation, income and the bond rate move money holdings by similar amounts.

exm-lm-money-omitted.title: Income without interest rates
exm-lm-money-omitted.html: Regressing log money on log income alone, with an intercept, gives an income elasticity of 1.819, against 1.2958 when both interest rates are included. @prp-lm-omitted(a) accounts for the whole difference. Regressing each rate on log income gives slopes −0.2215 (bond rate) and −0.0917 (deposit rate): in these data, quarters with higher income had lower interest rates, and the correlation of log income with the bond rate is −0.52. The short-regression elasticity therefore absorbs (−0.2215)(−2.6163)+(−0.0917)(0.6186)=0.5229, mostly the association of higher income with lower bond rates, which in turn go with more money. Which elasticity is the “right” one depends on the question. The long regression compares quarters with equal interest rates. The short one compares quarters as they came, with whatever rates accompanied a given income.

exm-lm-money-se.title: Standard errors for money demand
exm-lm-money-se.html:
For the money demand model of @exm-lm-money, n=55 and p=4, so s2=0.0925351=0.001814,s=0.04259. Since the response is a logarithm, s says that money holdings typically deviate from the fitted relation by about 4 percent. The standard errors of the four coefficients are 0.5811, 0.0940, 0.3282 and 0.6911. The income coefficient 1.2958 is almost fourteen standard errors from zero and the bond rate coefficient −2.6163 about eight, but the deposit rate coefficient 0.6186 is smaller than its standard error. Whether the deposit rate belongs in the model at all is a testing question for Chapter 11.

These standard errors rest on (L2) and (L3). For a quarterly economic series (L3) is doubtful. The correlation between consecutive residuals is 0.62, which suggests that the errors are positively correlated in time, and then the formula σ2(X⊤X)−1 usually understates the true variability. Chapter 21 shows how to detect and allow for this.

exm-lm-simple-matrix.title: The straight line again
exm-lm-simple-matrix.html:
For X=[1,x], X⊤X=(nnx¯nx¯∑ixi2),X⊤y=(ny¯∑ixiyi). The determinant is n∑ixi2−n2x¯2=nSxx, positive iff the xi are not all equal, which is exactly when rank(X)=2. Inverting, (X⊤X)−1=1nSxx(∑ixi2−nx¯−nx¯n)=(1n+x¯2Sxx−x¯Sxx−x¯Sxx1Sxx),{#eq-lm-simple-inverse}

using ∑ixi2=Sxx+nx¯2. The second entry of (X⊤X)−1X⊤y is (∑ixiyi−nx¯y¯)/Sxx=Sxy/Sxx, and the first is y¯−x¯Sxy/Sxx. This recovers @thm-lm-simple-ls, and @eq-lm-ls-decomposition reduces to @eq-lm-simple-decomposition.

exm-lm-skewed-errors.title: Skewed errors
exm-lm-skewed-errors.html: To see that normality plays no role in @thm-lm-moments, fit the quadratic E(Y)=β0+β1x+β2x2 at x=1,…,12, with 𝛃β=(2,0.5,−0.03)⊤ and errors that are centred exponential variables scaled to σ=1.5. These errors are strongly skewed. Over 100,000 simulated data sets, the averages of the three estimates are 1.9974, 0.5005 and −0.0300, and the simulated standard deviations are 1.5421, 0.5457 and 0.0409, against 1.5503, 0.5483 and 0.0411 from @eq-lm-cov-beta. Every entry of the simulated covariance matrix is within 0.011 of the formula, measured as a correlation. The formula also predicts that β^1 and β^2 have correlation −0.973, because the columns x and x2 are nearly collinear on 1,…,12. A slightly larger linear coefficient can be almost exactly compensated by a slightly more negative quadratic one.

exm-lm-two-processes.title: Same regression function, different models
exm-lm-two-processes.html: Figure 5.1.1 shows two simulated data sets with the same regression function m(x)=1+0.5x. In panel (a) the errors are normal with constant standard deviation 0.8. In panel (b) they are skewed to the right, and their standard deviation grows linearly in x, from 0.15 at x=0 to 2.65 at x=10. The curves show the conditional density of Y at three values of x. Both processes satisfy (L1), so least squares estimates the line without bias in both. Only process (a) satisfies (L2), so only there do the variance formulas of Section 5.5 apply as stated. In process (b) most points lie below the line, because the median of a right-skewed distribution is below its mean. The line is still the conditional mean.

exr-lm-add-case.title: C1
exr-lm-add-case.html: Let X have full rank and let a new case (x0,y0) be appended. Using @thm-mat-woodbury, show that the new estimate is 𝛃𝛃𝛃β^new=β^+(X⊤X)−1x0(y0−x0⊤β^)1+x0⊤(X⊤X)−1x0. Interpret: the estimate moves in proportion to the new case’s prediction error. This is the basis of recursive least squares; Chapter 10 treats the numerically stable version.

exr-lm-add-column.title: B1
exr-lm-add-column.html: Let X=[X1,x] have full rank, and let SSE1 and SSE be the residual sums of squares from regressing y on X1 and on X. Show that SSE≤SSE1, directly from @def-lm-least-squares. Deduce that R2 cannot decrease when a column is added to a model with an intercept.

exr-lm-bivariate-normal.title: A2
exr-lm-bivariate-normal.html: Let (X,Y) be bivariate normal with means μX,μY, standard deviations σX,σY>0 and correlation ρ. Use @thm-mvn-conditional to find m(x) and Var(Y∣X=x). Conclude that a random sample from this distribution satisfies (L1)–(L4) conditionally on the xi, with columns 1,x. What are 𝛃β and σ2?

exr-lm-blp-not-regression.title: C1
exr-lm-blp-not-regression.html: Let X∼N(0,1) and Y=X2. Find the best linear predictor β0+β1X of Y (@thm-rv-blp) and its error u. Show that E(u)=0 and Cov(u,X)=0, but E(u∣X)≠0. Explain why fitting a straight line to a large sample from this distribution estimates a well-defined population quantity even though (L1) fails for the columns 1,x, and why the second-moment theory of this chapter does not describe the sampling variability of the fitted slope.

exr-lm-centred-uncorrelated.title: B2
exr-lm-centred-uncorrelated.html: In the centred parameterization 𝛃E(Y)=α1+Xcβ1 of @prp-lm-centred, show that 𝛃Cov(α^,β^1)=0, Var(α^)=σ2/n and 𝛃Cov(β^1)=σ2(Xc⊤Xc)−1. Deduce that Var(β^0)=σ2(1/n+x¯⊤(Xc⊤Xc)−1x¯), which generalizes @cor-lm-simple-moments.

exr-lm-effect-coding.title: B1
exr-lm-effect-coding.html: For a factor with three levels and an intercept, write the model matrix rows under reference coding (level 3 as reference) and under effect coding. Find the nonsingular 3×3 matrix K with Xeffect=XrefK, and express the effect-coding coefficients in terms of the three level means μ1,μ2,μ3.

exr-lm-fahrenheit.title: A1
exr-lm-fahrenheit.html: In @exm-lm-elnino, suppose both temperatures are converted to degrees Fahrenheit, F=32+1.8C. What happens to the slope, the intercept, R2 and s? Answer using @prp-lm-reparameterization, noting that the response is also transformed.

exr-lm-harmonic-orthogonal.title: C1
exr-lm-harmonic-orthogonal.html: Let ti=i/m for i=0,…,m−1 (one full period sampled at m equally spaced points, with m≥5). Show that the columns 1,cos⁡2πt,sin⁡2πt,cos⁡4πt,sin⁡4πt are mutually orthogonal, and find their squared lengths. Conclude that for a whole number of periods the harmonic coefficients are estimated separately from each other and from the mean. Why is this not exactly the case in @exm-lm-co2?

exr-lm-hetero-tautology.title: A1
exr-lm-hetero-tautology.html: Let X take the values −1,0,1 with probability 1/3 each, and let Y=X2+XZ, where Z∼N(0,1) is independent of X. Find the regression function m and the error ε. Show that E(ε∣X)=0 and Cov(ε,X)=0, but that ε and X are not independent. Which of the layers (L1)–(L4) fail for a sample from this distribution, with the columns 1,x,x2?

exr-lm-inconsistent.title: C1
exr-lm-inconsistent.html: Let xi=1/i for i=1,2,… in the straight-line model. Show that Sxx converges to a finite limit as n→∞, so that Var(β^1) does not tend to zero. Then construct a sequence of designs, in which the points may change with n (for example, designs centred farther and farther from 0), with Sxx→∞ but x¯2/Sxx↛0, and decide whether the slope, the intercept, or both fail to be consistent.

exr-lm-interaction-centring.title: B2
exr-lm-interaction-centring.html: In @eq-lm-interaction, replace x2 by x2−c in both the main-effect column and the product. Find the new coefficients in terms of the old, and show that the fitted mean function is unchanged. For which c is the new coefficient of x1 the slope at the average value of x2?

exr-lm-jensen-design.title: B2
exr-lm-jensen-design.html: In @exm-lm-fixed-random the regressors are independent and uniform on [0,10]. Show that E(Sxx)=(n−1)⋅100/12. Use Jensen’s inequality to show that E(σ2/Sxx)≥σ2/E(Sxx), with strict inequality here. Why is the right side of no use for describing the precision of the slope from a given sample?

exr-lm-lad-line.title: C1
exr-lm-lad-line.html: The least absolute deviations line minimizes ∑i|yi−b0−b1xi|. Show that some minimizing line passes through at least two of the data points (assume the xi are not all equal). Hint: for fixed b1 the best b0 is a median of the yi−b1xi, and the objective is piecewise linear and convex in b1. Compare the effect of the 1997 point in @exm-lm-elnino on this line and on the least squares line.

exr-lm-leverage-simple.title: A2
exr-lm-leverage-simple.html: Show that for a straight line hii=1/n+(xi−x¯)2/Sxx. Which case in @exm-lm-elnino has the largest leverage? Check that the leverages sum to 2.

exr-lm-linear-estimator.title: B3
exr-lm-linear-estimator.html: Show that 𝛃β^=Ay with A=(X⊤X)−1X⊤, that AX=Ip, and that AA⊤=(X⊤X)−1. Give an example of a different p×n matrix B with BX=Ip when n>p. (Chapter 7 compares all such estimators By.)

exr-lm-linear-or-not.title: A2
exr-lm-linear-or-not.html: Which of these mean functions define linear models in the stated parameters (after a change of parameters if necessary)? (a) β0+β1x; (b) β0eβ1x; (c) β0+β1x+β2max(x−5,0); (d) β0+β1sin⁡(x−β2); (e) 1/(β0+β1x).

exr-lm-linear-probability.title: B1
exr-lm-linear-probability.html: Let Yi be binary with 𝛃Pr(Yi=1)=x(i)⊤β (the linear probability model). Show that (L1) holds but (L2) fails, with Var(Yi)=μi(1−μi). Show that least squares is still unbiased, find its covariance matrix from @prp-lm-misspecified(b), and explain why fitted values outside [0,1] are possible.

exr-lm-linear-weights.title: B1
exr-lm-linear-weights.html: Show that β^1=∑iciyi with ci=(xi−x¯)/Sxx, and that ∑ici=0, ∑icixi=1 and ∑ici2=1/Sxx. Write β^0 as ∑idiyi and find ∑idi, ∑idixi and ∑idi2.

exr-lm-mle-mse.title: B2
exr-lm-mle-mse.html: Under normality SSE/σ2 has mean n−p and variance 2(n−p). Among estimators c⋅SSE, find the c that minimizes the mean squared error E(cSSE−σ2)2. Compare with 1/(n−p) and 1/n.

exr-lm-omitted-sign.title: B3
exr-lm-omitted-sign.html: In a model with an intercept and two regressors, let the short regression omit x2. Show that the bias of the slope on x1 is β2S12/S11, where S12=∑i(xi1−x¯1)(xi2−x¯2) and S11=∑i(xi1−x¯1)2. Tabulate the sign of the bias according to the signs of β2 and the correlation of the two regressors.

exr-lm-optimal-design.title: B1
exr-lm-optimal-design.html: Suppose n is even and the xi may be chosen anywhere in [a,b]. Show that Sxx≤n(b−a)2/4, with equality iff half the points are at a and half at b. Hint: |xi−c|≤(b−a)/2 with c=(a+b)/2, and Sxx=∑i(xi−c)2−n(x¯−c)2.

exr-lm-origin-r2.title: A2
exr-lm-origin-r2.html: For regression through the origin, show that ∑iyi2=∑iy^i2+∑iε^i2, and give a small data set for which 1−∑iε^i2/∑iyi2 is close to 1 while 1−∑iε^i2/Syy is negative.

exr-lm-orthogonal-columns.title: A1
exr-lm-orthogonal-columns.html: Suppose the columns of X are nonzero and mutually orthogonal. Show that β^j=xj⊤y/xj⊤xj for each j, so that each coefficient is the same as in the regression of y on xj alone. Show also that deleting a column does not change the other estimates.

exr-lm-poisson-score.title: B2
exr-lm-poisson-score.html: For independent Yi∼Poisson(μi) with 𝛃log⁡μi=x(i)⊤β, write the log-likelihood and show that its gradient is 𝛍X⊤(y−μ). Deduce that when X contains an intercept the fitted means sum to ∑iyi, and that for the intercept-only model the fitted mean is y¯.

exr-lm-quadratic-unbiased.title: C1
exr-lm-quadratic-unbiased.html: Show that a quadratic form Y⊤AY with A symmetric is unbiased for σ2 for every 𝛃β and σ2 iff X⊤AX=0 and trA=1. Verify that A=(I−H)/(n−p) qualifies, and find another A that does. (Under normality, @thm-opt-umvue shows that s2 has the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators.)

exr-lm-s2-origin.title: A1
exr-lm-s2-origin.html: For regression through the origin, E(Yi)=βxi, what is the unbiased estimator of σ2? Verify E(SSE)=σ2(n−1) directly, by writing SSE=∑iεi2−(∑ixiεi)2/∑ixi2.

exr-lm-scale-model.title: C1
exr-lm-scale-model.html: In process (b) of @exm-lm-two-processes the error standard deviation is 0.15+0.25x. Suppose instead log⁡Var(Yi)=γ0+γ1xi with unknown γ. Propose a two-step procedure: fit the mean by least squares, then regress log⁡ε^i2 on xi. Show that, when the errors are normal and n→∞ with p fixed, the slope of the second regression estimates γ1 consistently, while its intercept estimates γ0+E(log⁡χ12). (Argue first with the errors εi in place of the residuals, then explain why the difference does not matter in the limit.) Compute this bias, −γE−log⁡2≈−1.27, where γE is Euler’s constant. (Chapter 45 treats models of this kind by likelihood, @def-qnt-gamlss.)

exr-lm-se-elnino.title: A2
exr-lm-se-elnino.html: For @exm-lm-elnino, compute s and the standard error of the slope. Is the slope more than two standard errors away from 1, the value that would mean December simply tracks August one for one?

exr-lm-sign-reversal.title: C1
exr-lm-sign-reversal.html: Construct a data set with n=8 cases, two regressors and an intercept, in which the slope of y on x1 is positive in the simple regression and negative in the regression on both x1 and x2. Explain the reversal with @prp-lm-omitted, and draw the scatterplot of y against x1 with the cases labelled by x2.

exr-lm-simple-small.title: A1
exr-lm-simple-small.html: For the five points (x,y)=(0,1),(1,1),(2,3),(3,4),(4,6), compute x¯,y¯,Sxx,Sxy, the least squares line, the residuals, and R2. Check the three identities of @prp-lm-simple-fit(a).

exr-lm-sse-formulas.title: B1
exr-lm-sse-formulas.html: Show that 𝛃𝛃SSE=y⊤y−β^⊤X⊤Xβ^, and that for a model with an intercept 𝛃𝛃SSE=Syy−β^1⊤Xc⊤Xcβ^1 in the notation of @prp-lm-centred. Explain why the second form is numerically preferable when the responses are large and nearly equal, as in @exm-lm-co2.

exr-lm-standardized.title: B1
exr-lm-standardized.html: Show that the standardized coefficients are the slopes obtained by regressing the standardized response (yi−y¯)/sy on the standardized regressors (xij−x¯j)/sxj, without an intercept. For a single regressor, show that the standardized slope is the correlation r.

exr-lm-two-group-var.title: A1
exr-lm-two-group-var.html: In the model of @prp-lm-indicator-means with c=2 groups, show that Var(β^1)=σ2(1/n1+1/n2), both from @eq-lm-cov-beta and directly from β^1=Y¯1−Y¯2. For fixed n=n1+n2, which split minimizes it?

exr-lm-var-difference.title: B2
exr-lm-var-difference.html: In @exm-lm-money, write the variances of β^2−β^3 and β^2+β^3, the difference and the sum of the two interest-rate coefficients, in terms of the entries of G=(X⊤X)−1. Show that if β^2 and β^3 are negatively correlated, the difference is estimated less precisely, and the sum more precisely, than they would be if the two estimates were uncorrelated. The two rate columns have sample correlation 0.80. Which combination would you expect to be better determined?

exr-lm-variance-explained.title: B1
exr-lm-variance-explained.html: Under the conditions of @prp-lm-error-decomposition, show that Var(Y)=Var(m(X))+E[Var(Y∣X)] and that E(ε2)=E[Var(Y∣X)]. The ratio η2=Var(m(X))/Var(Y) is the proportion of the variance of Y that the regression function explains. Compute it for the distribution of @exr-lm-hetero-tautology.

exr-lm-weighted.title: B2
exr-lm-weighted.html: Let W=diag(w1,…,wn) with all wi>0, and X of full rank. Show that ∑iwi(yi−x(i)⊤b)2 has the unique minimizer (X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wy, by applying @thm-lm-ls-full-rank to the rescaled data W1/2y and W1/2X. Which cases get most influence when the weights are the reciprocals of the error variances?

exr-lm-weighted-mean-slopes.title: B2
exr-lm-weighted-mean-slopes.html: Suppose all xi are distinct. Show that β^1 is a weighted average of the slopes (yj−yi)/(xj−xi) of the lines through all pairs of points, with weights proportional to (xj−xi)2. Hint: show that ∑i<j(xj−xi)(yj−yi)=nSxy and ∑i<j(xj−xi)2=nSxx.

exr-lm-which-model.title: A1
exr-lm-which-model.html: For each response, name the rung of the ladder you would start from, and say which of the three components (distribution, predictor, link) departs from the normal linear model: (a) whether a loan is repaid; (b) blood pressure measured monthly on the same patients; (c) the number of insurance claims per policy; (d) the 90th percentile of birth weight as a function of the mother’s age; (e) crop yield in a randomized block experiment.

exr-lm-write-X.title: A1
exr-lm-write-X.html: Write out the model matrix for each model, for the data x=(1,2,3,4) and a group label (A,A,B,B), and give its rank: (a) a quadratic in x; (b) separate intercepts for the two groups and a common slope; (c) separate lines in the two groups, with reference coding; (d) an intercept, an indicator for A and an indicator for B.

prp-lm-centred.title: Centred form
prp-lm-centred.html: Let X=[1,X1] have rank p=k+1, and partition 𝛃𝛃β^=(β^0,β^1⊤)⊤. Then Xc has rank k, and 𝛃𝛃β^1=(Xc⊤Xc)−1Xc⊤y=(Xc⊤Xc)−1Xc⊤(y−y¯1),β^0=y¯−x¯⊤β^1.

prp-lm-consistency.title: Consistency in mean square
prp-lm-consistency.html: Under the linear model with Xn of full rank p for every n, if tr(Xn⊤Xn)−1→0, equivalently if the smallest eigenvalue of Xn⊤Xn tends to infinity, then 𝛃𝛃E‖β^−β‖2→0, and hence 𝛃𝛃Pr(‖β^−β‖>δ)→0 for every δ>0.

prp-lm-error-decomposition.title: The error of the regression function
prp-lm-error-decomposition.title_html: The error of the regression function
prp-lm-error-decomposition.html:
Let EY2<∞, and let m and ε be as in @def-lm-regression-function.

  1. E(ε∣X)=0, and hence E(ε)=0.

  2. E[εg(X)]=0 for every function g with Eg(X)2<∞. In particular ε is uncorrelated with every such function of the regressors.

  3. For every such g, E[(Y−g(X))2]=E(ε2)+E[(m(X)−g(X))2]. So m(X) is the best predictor of Y from X in mean squared error, and it is the only one up to events of probability zero.

prp-lm-fit-algebra.title: Algebra of the fit
prp-lm-fit-algebra.html:
Let X have rank p, and let H, Y^ and 𝛆ε^ be as above.

  1. H is symmetric and idempotent, HX=X and (I−H)X=0, and trH=p, tr(I−H)=n−p.

  2. 𝛆X⊤ε^=0 and 𝛆Y^⊤ε^=0.

  3. 𝛆‖y‖2=‖Y^‖2+‖ε^‖2, and 𝛃SSE=y⊤(I−H)y=y⊤y−β^⊤X⊤y.

  4. If 1=Xc for some c (for example, if X has an intercept column), then ∑iε^i=0, the mean of the fitted values is y¯, and ∑i(yi−y¯)2=∑i(y^i−y¯)2+∑iε^i2, that is, SST=SSR+SSE.

  5. If 𝛃𝛆y=Xβ+ε for some 𝛃β and 𝛆ε, then 𝛃𝛃𝛆β^=β+(X⊤X)−1X⊤ε and 𝛆𝛆ε^=(I−H)ε.

prp-lm-fit-moments.title: Moments of fitted values and residuals
prp-lm-fit-moments.title_html: Moments of fitted values and residuals
prp-lm-fit-moments.html:
Under the linear model with X of full rank and H=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤:

  1. 𝛃E(Y^)=Xβ and Cov(Y^)=σ2H;

  2. 𝛆E(ε^)=0 and 𝛆Cov(ε^)=σ2(I−H); in particular Var(ε^i)=σ2(1−hii), where hii is the ith diagonal entry of H;

  3. 𝛆Cov(Y^,ε^)=0 and 𝛃𝛆Cov(β^,ε^)=0;

  4. 0≤hii≤1 for every i, and ∑ihii=p.

prp-lm-indicator-means.title: Coefficients of indicator variables
prp-lm-indicator-means.html: Suppose each case belongs to one of c≥2 groups, group k has nk≥1 cases with mean response y¯k, and zk is the indicator column of group k. Let X=[1,z1,…,zc−1], so that group c is the reference. Then X has full rank, and β^0=y¯c,β^k=y¯k−y¯c(k=1,…,c−1). The fitted value of every case is the mean of its group.

prp-lm-misspecified.title: Moments under departures
prp-lm-misspecified.html:
Let X have full rank, A=(X⊤X)−1X⊤ and 𝛃β^=AY.

  1. If 𝛃𝛅E(Y)=Xβ+δ for some 𝛅δ∈Rn, then 𝛃𝛃𝛅E(β^)=β+(X⊤X)−1X⊤δ.

  2. If 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=Σ for some covariance matrix Σ, then 𝛃𝛃E(β^)=β and 𝛃Cov(β^)=(X⊤X)−1X⊤ΣX(X⊤X)−1.{#eq-lm-sandwich}

prp-lm-omitted.title: Omitted regressors
prp-lm-omitted.html:
Let X=[X1,X2] have full rank, and let Π=(X1⊤X1)−1X1⊤X2 be the coefficient matrix from regressing each column of X2 on X1. Then:

  1. for every data vector y, 𝛃𝛃𝛃β~1=β^1+Πβ^2;

  2. if 𝛃𝛃E(Y)=X1β1+X2β2, then 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(β~1)=β1+Πβ2.

In particular the short and long coefficients agree, for all y, iff X1⊤X2=0.

prp-lm-reparameterization.title: Reparameterization
prp-lm-reparameterization.html: Let X be n×p of rank p, let K be a nonsingular p×p matrix, and put Z=XK. Then Z has rank p, and the least squares estimates from the two model matrices are related by 𝛃𝛃β^Z=K−1β^X. The fitted values, residuals, SSE and s2 are the same for both, and the estimated covariance matrices satisfy s2(Z⊤Z)−1=K−1[s2(X⊤X)−1](K−1)⊤.

prp-lm-simple-fit.title: Properties of the fitted line
prp-lm-simple-fit.html:
Under the conditions of @thm-lm-simple-ls:

  1. ∑iε^i=0, ∑ixiε^i=0 and ∑iy^iε^i=0;

  2. the line passes through (x¯,y¯), and the mean of the fitted values is y¯;

  3. with SST=Syy and SSR=∑i(y^i−y¯)2, SST=SSR+SSE,SSR=β^12Sxx=Sxy2Sxx, and so SSE=Syy−Sxy2/Sxx;

  4. if also Syy>0, the coefficient of determination R2=SSR/SST equals r2, the square of the sample correlation r=Sxy/SxxSyy.

prp-lm-var-s2.title: Variance of s²
prp-lm-var-s2.html: In the linear model with rank(X)=p<n, suppose the errors ε1,…,εn are independent with mean 0, variance σ2, common third moment μ3=E(εi3) and common fourth moment μ4=E(εi4)<∞. Then Var(SSE)=2σ4(n−p)+(μ4−3σ4)∑i=1n(1−hii)2. For normal errors, μ4=3σ4 and Var(s2)=2σ4/(n−p).

thm-lm-ls-full-rank.title: Least squares for a full-rank model
thm-lm-ls-full-rank.title_html: Least squares for a full-rank model
thm-lm-ls-full-rank.html:
Let X be an n×p matrix of rank p. Then:

  1. X⊤X is positive definite, and in particular nonsingular;

  2. the normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y{#eq-lm-normal-equations}

    have exactly one solution, 𝛃β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y;{#eq-lm-beta-hat}

  3. for every b∈Rp, 𝛃𝛃𝛃‖y−Xb‖2=‖y−Xβ^‖2+(b−β^)⊤X⊤X(b−β^),{#eq-lm-ls-decomposition}

    so 𝛃β^ is the unique least squares estimate.

If instead rank(X)<p, least squares estimates exist but are never unique.

thm-lm-moments.title: Moments of the least squares estimator
thm-lm-moments.title_html: Moments of the least squares estimator
thm-lm-moments.html:
Let X have full rank p and 𝛃β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤Y.

  1. If 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, then 𝛃𝛃E(β^)=β: the least squares estimator is unbiased.

  2. If moreover Cov(Y)=σ2In, then 𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2(X⊤X)−1.{#eq-lm-cov-beta}

thm-lm-sigma2.title: Unbiased estimation of the error variance
thm-lm-sigma2.title_html: Unbiased estimation of the error variance
thm-lm-sigma2.html:
In the linear model @def-lm-linear-model with rank(X)=p<n, E(SSE)=σ2(n−p). Hence 𝛃s2=SSEn−p=‖Y−Xβ^‖2n−p{#eq-lm-s2}

is an unbiased estimator of σ2.

thm-lm-simple-ls.title: Least squares for a straight line
thm-lm-simple-ls.title_html: Least squares for a straight line
thm-lm-simple-ls.html:
Suppose the xi are not all equal. Then S(b0,b1) has a unique minimizer (β^0,β^1), given by β^1=SxySxx,β^0=y¯−β^1x¯.{#eq-lm-simple-estimates}

It is the unique solution of the two normal equations ∑i=1n(yi−b0−b1xi)=0,∑i=1nxi(yi−b0−b1xi)=0.{#eq-lm-simple-normal}

Moreover, for all b0,b1, S(b0,b1)=S(β^0,β^1)+n[(b0−β^0)+(b1−β^1)x¯]2+Sxx(b1−β^1)2.{#eq-lm-simple-decomposition}
